extracted.intended_audience: improv performers, teachers, directors and comedy students
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and evaluative criteria for performing, directing, teaching and producing improvisational comedy (long- and short-form), drawn from an interview with an experienced improviser/director. Covers craft choices, training, career decisions, and commercial considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agree to the circumstances (baseline)
rubrics_metrics.description: Immediately agree to the circumstances or reality of a space presented to you in an improv scene (e.g., if you ask for a hammer, accept the hardware-store reality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agreement to circumstances is a foundational, quickly teachable baseline — Napier says it's "easy enough to teach in about thirty minutes." Use it as the starting point for a scene, but not as the only tool.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't over-rely on "Yes, and..."
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid treating 'Yes, and...' as the root of good improvisation; over-hyping it can leave performers weak and tentative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Napier critiques the hyped 'Yes, and...' pattern: performers who merely agree and add a little content can appear powerless. Teach/encourage other tactics (edge, irony, disagreement) rather than mechanical agreement-plus-addition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use disagreement and conflict as a strength
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters may disagree or be aggressive in ways that create strong, interesting scenes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disagreement, irony, or a 'wicked' perspective can provide power and edge. Napier notes many great scenes come from characters opposing each other rather than always affirming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bring power/edge/irony to choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Performances should have an underlying edge, irony, or strong character viewpoint rather than tentative, neutral additions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If performers feel weak after saying 'Yes, and...', encourage stronger stakes, ironic attitudes, or sharper character choices to give lines more impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality / avoid recycled premises
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware of whether a comedic premise has been done before; originality matters and casts/directors should detect repeats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Napier admits he relies on his cast to tell him when 'we're visiting a comedic premise that’s been visited before.' Directors/teams should cultivate awareness of overused premises and push for fresh angles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance training with practical doing (diminishing returns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive classes/workshops can lead performers to be 'in their head' and experience diminishing returns after heavy investment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Napier cites personal experience: after spending about two grand on improv classes performers can become over-intellectualized. Encourage practice/performing and self-directed work alongside classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-training for a well-rounded improviser
rubrics_metrics.description: Exposure to multiple schools/styles (Annoyance, iO, UCB, Second City, etc.) creates a fuller, more well-rounded actor/improviser.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Napier observes that many in Chicago go through several institutions and that this cultural reinforcement produces a broader skill set; encourage sampling different approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid complacency from team membership
rubrics_metrics.description: Being on a team can feel satisfying and cause performers to neglect pursuing their own career or creative development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Directors and teachers should warn performers against stagnation: regular self-driven projects and career-focused effort are necessary to avoid six years passing with little personal progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand differences between long form and short/form sketch
rubrics_metrics.description: Long form and short form (games/sketches) are distinct: long form often builds narrative, whereas sketch/comedy can be unrelated scenes, monologues, songs, or shorter games.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize where your work sits (Harold, narrative musicals, sketch revue) and use suitable techniques. Napier notes Annoyance does more narrative works and musicals, while Second City focuses on sketch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rehearsal and production time expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Different production models require different time investments (e.g., weekly college sketch shows vs. two-month Second City Mainstage rehearsals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan schedules and expectations accordingly: creating an hour-long weekly show requires intense, frequent work; Mainstage processes can take months to refine material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directorial vigilance about repeated material
rubrics_metrics.description: Directors should be aware of material reuse and rely on performers to flag when a premise or joke has been seen before.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Napier admits sometimes he feels 'out of it' and depends on cast knowledge; cultivate an ensemble culture where team members surface potential repeats and influences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial viability / acceptable hit rate
rubrics_metrics.description: Top improvisers have an approximate 75% hit rate: three out of four scenes will be great and one will not, which factors into commercial viability decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use realistic expectations when producing improvised shows or pitching them for TV/film: consider whether the hit rate and variability are acceptable for the intended market or format.

rubrics_metrics.name: Career timing and marketability (age/training tradeoffs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Extended training pipelines can increase the average age of Mainstage actors, which may make them less marketable for some markets (e.g., Los Angeles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be strategic about timing career moves; prolonged time in training programs can unintentionally 'age' performers out of certain opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical innovation and creation skills
rubrics_metrics.description: Creating innovative work involves skills beyond performance: how to conduct meetings, present/pitch ideas, understand the psychology of creation, and handle internal obstacles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Napier's forthcoming book topics (conducting meetings, pitching, 'inner demons', presentation) suggest that production and collaborative skills are essential; include training on meeting dynamics, pitching techniques and group creativity processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teachability: basic vs advanced tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: Some elements (basic agreement) are quickly teachable while deeper tactics and styles require prolonged practice and experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure curricula to teach basics quickly, then allocate time for developing power, disagreement, irony, narrative craft and other advanced tactics that cannot be learned in a single session.
